sentences.text: Austriadraco dallavecchiai is an extinct genus of pterosaur known for its small size, with a humerus measuring about four centimetres.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a partial and disarticulated skeleton that includes a skull, vertebrae from the neck to the tail, and various limb bones.
Anatomical proportions show the shoulder blade is 62% longer than the coracoid, while the shinbone reaches 70% of the humerus length.
Early analysis incorrectly identified the fused frontal bones as a breast bone.
Bernd Lammerer discovered the skeleton in June 1994 on a mountain trail near Seefeld in Austrian Tirol at an altitude of 1600 metres.
The fossil remains were recovered as five stone plates from the Seefeld Formation dating from the late Norian.
In 2003, Peter Wellnhofer initially identified the fossil as a juvenile specimen of Eudimorphodon ranzii because it was 10 to 25% shorter than the holotype of that species.
Alexander Kellner named the genus Austriadraco in 2015, designating Austriadraco dallavecchiai as the type species, where the name combines the Latin words for Austria and dragon.

Kellner placed Austriadraco in an undefined family called Austriadraconidae due to uncertain affinities, suggesting a close relationship with Arcticodactylus based on the shared trait of a short coracoid.
A 2020 study by Matthew G. Baron grouped Austriadraco with Carniadactylus and Raeticodactylus within the clade Caviramidae, noting its closest relative may have been Eudimorphodon or Arcticodactylus.
Austriadraco lived during the Late Triassic, specifically the Norian stage between 217 and 213 million years ago, in present-day Austria.
It is debated whether the specimen represents a juvenile of Eudimorphodon or a distinct genus, with Dalla Vecchia concluding it was neither in 2009.
